blocks.text: A 30-year-old stands up quickly from a hospital bed after a night of lying flat. For a second the room swims, then it passes. In that second, about half a litre of blood has pooled in the veins of the legs and arterial pressure at the head has dipped, and a reflex arc lasting only a few heartbeats has corrected it. Longer-term control of the same pressure is handed to the kidney and hormones.

blocks.markdown:
Arterial pressure is the driving force for blood flow through the organs, so it is regulated tightly. Because pressure equals flow multiplied by resistance, mean arterial pressure (MAP) is determined by cardiac output (CO) and total peripheral resistance (TPR). The body uses two layers of control. **Fast neural reflexes** (seconds) adjust heart rate, contractility and vascular tone. **Slower hormonal and renal mechanisms** (hours to days) adjust blood volume, which sets cardiac output and therefore the long-term pressure.

A cuff measurement gives two numbers: systolic pressure (SBP, the peak during ventricular ejection) and diastolic pressure (DBP, the trough before the next ejection). Their difference is the pulse pressure (PP), which reflects stroke volume and arterial stiffness. For organ perfusion, the time-averaged pressure matters most.

blocks.title: Mean arterial pressure
blocks.text: MAP is the average arterial pressure across one cardiac cycle, in mmHg. Because the heart spends about one third of the cycle in systole and two thirds in diastole at resting heart rates, MAP is closer to diastolic than to systolic pressure. It is the pressure that drives perfusion of organs such as the brain and kidney.

blocks.caption: Estimated MAP in mmHg from cuff values. The second form is algebraically identical.

blocks.title: Calculating mean arterial pressure
blocks.prompt: A patient has blood pressure 126/78 mmHg. Calculate pulse pressure and MAP.

steps.text: One third of pulse pressure: 48 / 3 = 16 mmHg.
Check with the second form: (126 + 2 x 78) / 3 = (126 + 156) / 3 = 282 / 3 = 94 mmHg, which agrees.

blocks.answer: Pulse pressure 48 mmHg and MAP 94 mmHg. Note MAP is nearer the diastolic than the systolic value.

blocks.markdown:
**The baroreceptor reflex.** Baroreceptors are stretch-sensitive endings in the walls of the carotid sinus (afferents travel in the carotid sinus branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve, cranial nerve IX) and the aortic arch (afferents travel in the vagus nerve, cranial nerve X). They fire continuously, and firing rate rises when arterial pressure and wall stretch rise. Afferent signals end in the nucleus tractus solitarius in the medulla, which integrates them and controls autonomic outflow.

When pressure **falls**, baroreceptor firing falls. The medulla responds by reducing parasympathetic (vagal) outflow to the heart and increasing sympathetic outflow. The effects are: faster heart rate (less vagal braking, more sympathetic drive to the sinoatrial node), greater contractility, arteriolar constriction (raising TPR), venoconstriction (raising venous return and preload) and adrenal medullary release of adrenaline. Together these raise cardiac output and TPR, and so pressure returns towards the set point within seconds. The reflex resets in sustained hypertension, so it is a short-term buffer, not a long-term controller.

blocks.title: Tracking a fall in pressure through the reflex
blocks.prompt: On standing quickly, MAP at the carotid sinus drops from 93 to 78 mmHg. Trace the reflex response and the direction of each variable.

steps.text: Less stretch on carotid and aortic baroreceptors reduces their firing rate.
The nucleus tractus solitarius detects reduced firing and reduces vagal outflow while sympathetic outflow rises.
Heart rate and contractility rise, increasing cardiac output (CO = HR x SV).
Arteriolar and venous constriction raise TPR and venous return, further increasing MAP (MAP = CO x TPR approximately).
MAP rises back towards 93 mmHg, baroreceptor firing recovers, and the reflex stabilises (negative feedback).

blocks.answer: Reduced baroreceptor firing leads to increased sympathetic and decreased parasympathetic outflow, which raises heart rate, contractility and vascular resistance and restores pressure within seconds.

blocks.markdown:
**The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS).** The juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney release the enzyme renin in response to reduced renal perfusion pressure, reduced sodium chloride delivery to the macula densa and sympathetic stimulation through beta-1 receptors. Renin cleaves angiotensinogen (a plasma protein made by the liver) to angiotensin I. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), located on vascular endothelium and especially abundant in the lungs, converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II.

Angiotensin II acts at AT1 receptors to: (1) constrict arterioles, raising TPR; (2) stimulate aldosterone secretion from the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex; (3) promote thirst and antidiuretic hormone release; and (4) promote sodium reabsorption in the proximal tubule. Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption in the principal cells of the collecting duct, and water follows. The result is a larger extracellular volume, a larger venous return and a higher cardiac output, which raises pressure and ends renin release. This is the long-term mechanism: it works over hours to days and does not adapt.

blocks.caption: Comparison of the two main layers of arterial pressure control.
rows: Stretch receptors in carotid sinus and aortic arch
Juxtaglomerular cells and macula densa (renal perfusion, NaCl delivery)
Hours to days (angiotensin II vasoconstriction acts within minutes)
Raises blood volume and TPR; sustains pressure
Does not reset; chronic activation can sustain high pressure

items: Pressure falls (for example blood loss or standing).
Baroreceptor firing drops; sympathetic outflow rises and vagal outflow falls within seconds.
Renal perfusion falls and sympathetic beta-1 stimulation releases renin.
Angiotensin II constricts arterioles; aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone retain sodium and water.
Blood volume and cardiac output are restored and renin release falls (negative feedback).

blocks.title: Short term versus long term
blocks.text: The baroreceptor reflex corrects pressure within seconds by changing heart rate, contractility and vascular tone, but it adapts. The RAAS, together with the renal handling of sodium and water, sets blood volume and so determines the level at which long-term pressure is held.

blocks.title: MAP is not the simple average
blocks.text: The average of 120 and 80 is 100, but MAP is about 93 mmHg because diastole occupies roughly two thirds of the cycle at resting rates. At fast heart rates diastole shortens and the formula becomes less accurate, since MAP then moves closer to the arithmetic mean.

points: MAP = DBP + one third of pulse pressure = (SBP + 2 x DBP) / 3, and it is the perfusion pressure for organs.
The baroreceptor reflex (carotid sinus via cranial nerve IX, aortic arch via cranial nerve X) responds to a fall in pressure with reduced vagal and increased sympathetic outflow.
Renin from the kidney leads to angiotensin II (via ACE) and aldosterone, which constrict arterioles and retain sodium and water, restoring blood volume.
The reflex acts within seconds but adapts; the RAAS and renal volume control sustain pressure over days.

questions.stem: A man loses blood from a laceration and his arterial pressure falls. Which immediate autonomic change is produced by the baroreceptor reflex?

options.text: Decreased parasympathetic and increased sympathetic outflow
Increased parasympathetic and decreased sympathetic outflow
Increased parasympathetic and increased sympathetic outflow to the heart
No change in autonomic outflow until renin is released

questions.correctOptionText: Decreased parasympathetic and increased sympathetic outflow

distractorRationale.a: Correct: reduced baroreceptor firing withdraws vagal tone and increases sympathetic drive.
distractorRationale.b: This would slow the heart and dilate vessels, which would lower pressure further.
distractorRationale.c: The two limbs of the autonomic system change in opposite directions in this reflex.
distractorRationale.d: The baroreceptor reflex acts within seconds, long before renin-mediated changes.

questions.explanation: A fall in arterial pressure reduces baroreceptor firing to the nucleus tractus solitarius. The medulla then reduces vagal outflow and increases sympathetic outflow, raising heart rate, contractility and vascular resistance. This is a fast negative feedback response.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly matches a baroreceptor site with the nerve carrying its afferent signals to the medulla?

options.text: Carotid sinus with glossopharyngeal nerve; aortic arch with vagus nerve
Carotid sinus with vagus nerve; aortic arch with glossopharyngeal nerve
Carotid sinus with trigeminal nerve; aortic arch with vagus nerve
Carotid sinus with glossopharyngeal nerve; aortic arch with phrenic nerve

questions.correctOptionText: Carotid sinus with glossopharyngeal nerve; aortic arch with vagus nerve

distractorRationale.a: Correct: carotid sinus afferents travel in cranial nerve IX and aortic arch afferents travel in cranial nerve X.
distractorRationale.b: The nerves are reversed in this option.
distractorRationale.c: The trigeminal nerve carries facial sensation, not baroreceptor signals.
distractorRationale.d: The phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm and is not a baroreceptor afferent.

questions.explanation: Carotid sinus baroreceptors send their signals through the carotid sinus branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve, while aortic arch baroreceptors use the vagus nerve. Both pathways end in the nucleus tractus solitarius of the medulla.

questions.stem: Which stimulus increases renin release from juxtaglomerular cells?

options.text: Raised arterial pressure at the afferent arteriole
Raised plasma angiotensin II acting on the juxtaglomerular cells
Increased sodium chloride delivery to the macula densa

distractorRationale.a: Correct: reduced stretch of the afferent arteriole stimulates renin release.
distractorRationale.b: Raised pressure stretches the arteriole and suppresses renin.
distractorRationale.c: Angiotensin II inhibits renin release in a negative feedback loop.
distractorRationale.d: Increased NaCl delivery to the macula densa suppresses renin; decreased delivery stimulates it.

questions.explanation: Renin is released when renal perfusion pressure falls, when sodium chloride delivery to the macula densa falls, and with sympathetic beta-1 stimulation. Conditions that signal adequate pressure or volume, including raised angiotensin II, suppress it.

questions.stem: Angiotensin I is converted to the active vasoconstrictor angiotensin II mainly by which enzyme and at which site?

options.text: Angiotensin-converting enzyme on vascular endothelium, particularly in the lungs
Renin in the juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney
Aldosterone synthase in the adrenal cortex
Carbonic anhydrase in the red blood cell

questions.correctOptionText: Angiotensin-converting enzyme on vascular endothelium, particularly in the lungs

distractorRationale.a: Correct: ACE cleaves angiotensin I to angiotensin II and is abundant on pulmonary capillary endothelium.
distractorRationale.b: Renin cleaves angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, an earlier step.
distractorRationale.c: Aldosterone synthase makes aldosterone, not angiotensin II.
distractorRationale.d: Carbonic anhydrase handles CO2 hydration and has no role here.

questions.explanation: Renin produces angiotensin I from angiotensinogen, and angiotensin-converting enzyme then produces angiotensin II. ACE is found on vascular endothelium throughout the body and is particularly abundant in pulmonary capillaries.

questions.stem: True or false: When arterial pressure falls, the firing rate of carotid sinus baroreceptors increases.
questions.explanation: Baroreceptors are stretch receptors, so their firing rate rises when pressure and wall stretch rise and falls when pressure falls. It is this fall in firing that triggers the compensatory sympathetic activation.

questions.stem: A patient's blood pressure is 150/96 mmHg. Calculate the mean arterial pressure in mmHg.
questions.explanation: Pulse pressure is 150 - 96 = 54 mmHg, and one third of it is 18 mmHg. MAP = DBP + 18 = 96 + 18 = 114 mmHg. The equivalent form (150 + 2 x 96) / 3 = 342 / 3 = 114 mmHg gives the same answer.

questions.stem: After severe blood loss a patient's blood pressure is 84/52 mmHg. Calculate the mean arterial pressure in mmHg, to one decimal place.
questions.explanation: Pulse pressure is 84 - 52 = 32 mmHg, and one third is 10.7 mmHg. MAP = 52 + 10.7 = 62.7 mmHg. A value around 60 mmHg is near the lower limit at which organ perfusion becomes threatened, which is why the baroreflex and RAAS are activated.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old stands abruptly from lying flat and feels briefly light-headed. Describe the baroreceptor reflex response that restores arterial pressure, naming the sensors, afferent nerves, integrating centre and effectors.
markingGuide: Standing pools blood in the legs, reducing venous return, cardiac output and arterial pressure
Reduced stretch of carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors lowers their firing rate
Afferents travel in the glossopharyngeal (carotid) and vagus (aortic) nerves to the nucleus tractus solitarius in the medulla
Vagal outflow falls and sympathetic outflow rises
Effects: higher heart rate and contractility, arteriolar constriction raising resistance, venoconstriction raising venous return
Pressure is restored within seconds (negative feedback)
questions.explanation: Pooling of blood in the legs lowers venous return and arterial pressure, which reduces baroreceptor firing. The medulla then reduces vagal outflow and raises sympathetic outflow so that heart rate, contractility and vascular tone increase. Pressure returns towards the set point within a few seconds.

questions.stem: Explain how the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system raises and sustains arterial pressure after a prolonged fall in blood volume. Include the stimulus for renin, the role of angiotensin II and aldosterone, and why this system acts over a longer time course than the baroreceptor reflex.
markingGuide: Stimulus: reduced renal perfusion pressure, reduced NaCl at the macula densa and sympathetic beta-1 stimulation release renin from juxtaglomerular cells
Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I; ACE converts it to angiotensin II
Angiotensin II causes arteriolar vasoconstriction, thirst, ADH release and aldosterone secretion
Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption in the collecting duct, with water following, expanding blood volume
Increased volume raises venous return, cardiac output and pressure; renin falls by negative feedback
Acts over hours to days because it depends on hormone synthesis and renal handling of salt and water, and it does not adapt like the baroreflex
questions.explanation: Reduced renal perfusion and sympathetic activity release renin, which produces angiotensin II via ACE. Angiotensin II constricts arterioles and drives aldosterone secretion, which causes the kidney to retain sodium and water. Because this depends on hormone synthesis and renal volume handling, it takes hours to days, but it does not reset and so sustains pressure.

questions.stem: A clinic reading is 138/72 mmHg. Calculate the mean arterial pressure, and explain why MAP is closer to the diastolic than the systolic value and why it is clinically useful.
markingGuide: At resting heart rates diastole lasts about twice as long as systole, so the time-averaged pressure is nearer diastolic
MAP is the average perfusion pressure driving flow to organs, so it identifies inadequate perfusion
May note the formula is less accurate at fast heart rates
questions.explanation: Pulse pressure is 66 mmHg, so MAP = 72 + 22 = 94 mmHg. The ventricle spends about two thirds of the cycle in diastole at resting rates, so the average pressure is weighted towards the diastolic value. MAP matters because it is the effective driving pressure for organ perfusion.
